stories.title: Orange Order seeks urgent meetings over parade decision
stories.summary: The Orange Order is seeking urgent meetings following the banning of its parade on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown following an almost two-week stand-off. British Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant said that it had not been possible to find accommodation between the Orange Order and the residents of Garvaghy Road, leading to the contentious parade being banned. In a statement, he said that the decision was made in "the interests of wider public interest and safety". "I heard the concerns of people on all sides and I only regret that we could not reach a compromise on a way forward and that many residents across Portadown have felt anxious and worried," he said. "With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions." Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill welcomed the decision to halt the parade along the Garvaghy Road, but unionist politicians have criticised the move.

stories.title: Dáil sitting days may be moved over planned strike
stories.summary: Dáil votes could take place next Tuesday night instead of on the usual day of Wednesday because of a national strike day. It is also understood that Dáil sitting days could be moved to accommodate the one-day public sector strike next Wednesday which would inhibit business in the Oireachtas. This means that it is possible that the Dáil could sit next Friday instead of Wednesday. Public sector unions have accused the Government of failing to make a meaningful offer on pay and are planning large-scale strike action on 14 October. More than 300,000 public sector workers are to strike on Wednesday, in the biggest day of national strike action since the aftermath of the 2008 economic crash. Among the protests planned is a picket line at Leinster House, where the Dáil is scheduled to sit.

stories.title: Polanski vows to stay Greens leader despite election loss
stories.summary: Zack Polanski has insisted he will carry on as Greens leader despite failing to win a seat in Parliament as the fallout continued from the party conference backing a motion declaring Zionism is racism. The UK Green Party leader's position was being questioned by senior colleagues even before he was unsuccessful in ousting Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election triggered by the resignation of former prime minister Keir Starmer. Mr Polanski said "of course I can carry on" as party leader but acknowledged that ultimately Green members would decide his fate. He was defeated by Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, who retained the north London seat for Labour. She secured 45% of the vote to the Greens' 33%, a majority of 3,364 but seeing a 13% swing to the Greens, whose vote share was up by 22.4%. Mr Polanski missed the Green Party conference vote which endorsed a policy effectively calling for Israel to be abolished and replaced with a single Palestinian state.

stories.title: Waterford residents to stage protest against data centre
stories.summary: Local residents and farmers are set to stage a protest against a major data centre and energy development proposed for Kilmeaden, Co Waterford. The protest will see a convoy of cars, tractors, vans and other vehicles set off from Ballyduff National School this morning. The convoy will travel through Kilmeaden by way of Kildermody towards the Kingsmeadow Roundabout on the Cork Road, before returning through the village. Crag Rathnew DC Limited and Kent Homes Limited are seeking permission to develop the former Kilmeaden cheese factory site and its adjoining lands. The planning application states that the proposed development would "provide for a mixed use village centre, technology park, and renewable energy development on a total site area of 108.79 hectares." Those behind the project have said that all of their facilities are designed and developed in line with regulatory guidelines and in consultation with community representatives.

stories.title: 7.6 magnitude earthquake felt in Panama - USGS
stories.summary: A strong 7.6 magnitude earthquake struck near the southern coast of Panama at a 10km depth, according to the US Geological Survey. There were no immediate reports of damage in Panama, while television footage showed people evacuating buildings. The earthquake was downgraded from an earlier estimate of 8.0 magnitude. Tremors were felt in Panama City, where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets. Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the earthquake's impact. "We felt it very strongly," said one resident from the Herrera province, where the earthquake struck.

stories.title: Lonergan savouring best month of his footballing life
stories.summary: Tommy Lonergan struggled to sum it all up after an astonishing week in his career ended with him scoring a goal that helped Waterford reach the FAI Cup final. Lonergan was in Turners Cross on Tuesday, scoring a brace against England as the Ireland U21s secured a Euro 2027 play-off spot. And the 22-year-old was on target again at Dalymount Park, finding the back of the net as the Blues secured their spot in the biggest day in Irish soccer for the first time in 22 years following a 2-1 win over Bohemians. "Since I woke up this morning I've been very nervous about the game and I can't describe what this means to me. "What this club means to me and getting these fans to a cup final, it's one of the greatest moments of my life and I'm just so happy we got it over the line." Lonergan reserved particular praise for his manager Graham Coughlan, who has performed wonders with a side that were languishing at the bottom of the Premier Division before he arrived.

stories.title: Busy Wylde aiming to add to club medal haul
stories.summary: Plenty of players all around Ireland are preparing for county finals this weekend, but Sinéad Wylde is taking it one step further. stories.title: Cullen excited by return to Leinster's 'quirky' home
stories.summary: It feels like an age since Leinster last hosted a competitive game at the RDS, a URC quarter-final against Connacht in late May, 2024. Just over 26 months and a €52m redevelopment later, Leo Cullen's side will finally get to run out at what is now called the Laya Arena, which is expected to come close to hitting its 20,500 capacity for its full opening against Cardiff on Saturday. They didn't have to move far during their two seasons away. In fact, they didn't even have to leave Ballsbridge, as they set up shop at Aviva Stadium, occasionally venturing to Croke Park. The Aviva is a great place to play, but it's not home. And as they prepare for their first home game of the new season, the Leinster head coach is excited about getting back to their new and improved - but still "quirky" venue. "It's an insane amount of rugby clubs in a very small area, and then we're playing in the showjumping arena, playing rugby. "So it's an amazing thing, because obviously my mum breeds horses and ponies, as some of you may well be aware of. So I've been going there since I was literally a baby.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Elizabeth Magill's cultural picks
stories.summary: Northern Sky is an exhibition of new paintings by artist Elizabeth Magill at Dublin's Kerlin Gallery. Magill is one of the Kerlin's longest-standing artist collaborations, established when the gallery first opened in 1988. Since then, she has enjoyed a celebrated international career, exhibiting in multiple public and commercial galleries across UK, Europe and Asia. Of the paintings in Northern Sky, novelist Colm Tóibín writes: "The drama is these paintings is released and withheld. Sometimes there is wind; sometimes there is stillness. What is plain sits uneasily beside what is visionary. There is no simple meaning; instead, there is much ambiguity and strange, coiled beauty. Something might be about to happen, but that possibility is contained. It is as though the landscape is holding its breath and releasing its breath." A recent film I liked was called Blue Heron by a Canadian director called Sophy Romvari about her dysfunctional brother and how that impacted the whole family. Recently on Netflix, I watched a couple of good films: Harvest, an adaptation of a book by Jim Crace and another one called First They Killed My Father about the war in Cambodia from a child's perspective. The title of my current exhibition at the Kerlin Gallery came from a song written and performed by the late Nick Drake. I chose it because of his beautiful lyrics and voice, but also with my paintings I was trying to convey the stark luminosity you sometimes experience from skies in a northern hemisphere. My previous show was called By This River, from a Brian Eno song whereby all my painting were from his lyrics. But I’m drawn to many different types of music… too many to mention. I just finished, Chloe Iridjis' The Shadow of the Object, and I’m reading London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe, both very different books. Irdjis’ novel is nuanced and quietly powerful and Radden Keefe is fast-paced and based on a true family tragedy alongside the ever flowing river Thames and the distortions created by excessive wealth in the 80’s and 90’s London.

stories.summary: Baz Ashmawy told Patrick Kielty on Friday's Late Late Show that he and partner Tanja Evans "snuck off and got married in April" after 20 years together. stories.title: Irish designer Sasha Donnellan on finding her calling in Paris
stories.summary: Ellen Corcoran meets with Sasha Donnellan, the Irish designer who has captivated celebrity clients like Laura Whitmore and Roz Purcell, ahead of a dazzling presentation of her work during Paris Fashion Week. In the foyer of Hôtel Le Marois, I meet an elated and energetic Sasha Donnellan. She has a suitcase full of garments to bring back to Ireland ahead of her Ireland Fashion Week show in Dublin on Sunday morning, where she will showcase her full 20-look collection. The crowd finally fizzles out of the building and we find a seat by a grand piano as she catches her breath. Just 15 minutes earlier, a glimpse of her brand new collection, 'The Calling', had graced the runway for the very first time as part of Flying Solo NYC’s Paris Fashion Week show. Naturally, I ask how she’s feeling. "I was very nervous, of course, but also excited to see how people would perceive it, because I think this collection is quite different to my previous work", she says. "I feel like previous collections were much more focused on silks, and this time, I really leaned into my outerwear interest. That's something I haven't done before. So I was excited to see how people would react." Sasha refers to each of her collections as "little chapters" of her life. "I’m a designer, I love storytelling. To me, each collection represents a chapter that reflects something I'm incredibly passionate about at that moment." This time, that meant exploring the idea of a calling. Following her hugely successful Ireland Fashion Week debut in 2025, Sasha made the decision to become independent and commit fully to working on her brand, a move that prompted her to think about the people throughout history who had followed their own sense of purpose.

stories.title: Trump says Russia to supply diesel to US amid criticism
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has said that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort ⁠to lower fuel prices and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. Prices for diesel, used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, have increased and pose a risk for Mr Trump's fellow Republicans ahead of the 3 November congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain thin control of Congress. Diesel prices fell after the announcement, but analysts said the deal may not be enough to keep them down. Mr Trump said on social media he had a "highly successful" discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin in which they agreed that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets, equal to about 2.25million barrels of fuel. After the call, an envoy for Mr Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, praised cooperation between Russia and the US in a post on X. Mr Dmitriev asked US officials during his visit to Washington last month for licenses to export diesel to the US market to be granted to all Russian major oil firms, sources familiar with the situation said.

stories.title: EU meeting highlights aid role as other doners scale back
stories.summary: The EU has become the biggest provider of global development assistance after the Trump administration drastically cut back its international aid budget in 2025. A meeting of EU development ministers in Dublin today brought together representatives responsible for 80% of global development funding. The ministers were joined by counterparts from Canada, the United Kingdom, Norway, Iceland and the United Nations. The informal meeting heard that between 500,000-700,000 people around the world are estimated to have died since the US cuts to it aid programme came into effect. ''It has caused lives to be lost, but it's also seen a real backsliding on human rights, dignity, and values that so much work has put into,'' said Neale Richmond, Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs. Delegates were told of a "contagion effect" that has seen development assistance significantly reduced beyond the US, including in several EU member countries that were once considered dependable aid contributors.

stories.title: SF, People Before Profit representatives get PSNI letters
stories.summary: Sinn Féin and People Before Profit elected representatives in Northern Ireland have received letters from police probing alleged criminal offences in the ongoing parading dispute in Portadown. In a statement, Sinn Féin said a number of representatives and party members have received correspondence from police in relation to protests on the Garvaghy Road. It said the party "stood with the residents of the Garvaghy Road for the last two weeks in the face of provocation and the threat of an unwanted Orange march through their community". Earlier, People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll said he has been invited to attend a voluntary interview under caution in connection with protests on the Garvaghy Road. In a statement, he said he will be seeking the advice of his solicitor, adding: "Standing up for what's right is never wrong." The Police Service of Northern Ireland said individuals "reasonably suspected of committing offences" would receive letters for interview.

stories.title: DCC Energy to sell tech unit Nexora for $725m
stories.summary: Energy distributor DCC Energy said today it would sell its technology division, Nexora, to private equity firm One Equity Partners for a total enterprise value of $725m on a cash- and debt-free basis. The sale of the business is expected to complete on or after March 1, 2027, subject to regulatory approvals, DCC said in a statement. DCC agreed to a £5.75 billion takeover by a consortium of US private equity firms KKR and Energy Capital Partners in July. DCC said its shareholders will receive an additional 42 pence per share on top of the existing offer from the KKR-led consortium. But if regulatory conditions related to the sale of Nexora are not met by July 31, 2027, the additional consideration will be zero, it added. Donal Murphy, the chief executive of DCC Energy, said Nexora has been an important part of the DCC Group for many years and has built a strong market position through the expertise and commitment of its people.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned yesterday the war had reached a potentially explosive impasse, with the lack of a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation. "The other way that stalemates end is through escalation," Mr Rubio told reporters in Lisbon, warning that the conflict could spread to neighbouring NATO countries. "We do not believe that there is a military solution to this conflict," he said.

stories.title: Cup preview: Massive opportunity awaits Galway and Derry
stories.summary: The second Club Orange FAI Cup of the weekend takes place today, and it's Galway United and Derry City locking horns for the right to meet Waterford on Lansdowne Road next month. It should be a great occasion at Eamonn Deacy Park as Galway look to reach just their third ever decider against a Derry outfit who've claimed the title six times in four decades. The 'sold out' signs went up on the northside of Galway City in midweek, with around 5,000 expected to make the journey to Terryland. Neither club has covered themselves in glory in the league, but there's a massive prize to target, and it's just two wins away. While the Tribesman haven't been to Dublin 4 in 35 years, their manager John Caulfield is no stranger to the big day, having brought Cork City to the final in four consecutive years last decade. They won two of those four finals but it doing it with Galway would rank up there with any of those great days on Leeside.

stories.title: Horan succeeds McAleese as chair of Integration group
stories.summary: Former GAA president John Horan has been announced as the new chairperson of the Steering Group on Integration (SGI), replacing Dr Mary McAleese who recently stepped down from the role. Former President of Ireland Dr McAleese resigned as chairperson of the SGI last month, stating she was "dubious" that the amalgamation would successfully occur under the GAA's current leadership. She has now been replaced at the helm of the group by Horan, who served as the 39th president of the GAA. Separate leadership meetings of the three associations took place earlier this evening when the ratification of Horan as the new head of the SGI was sealed. A member of the Na Fianna club in Glasnevin, he was the first Dublin-born GAA president in 96 years. A retired secondary school principal at St Vincent's CBS, Glasnevin, Horan has built a long administrative career within the GAA.

stories.title: Dream big - inside The Ark's new anthology of plays for kids
stories.summary: Aideen Howard, creative director of The Ark, introduces Dream Big, the new book collecting a quintet of original (and acclaimed) theatre works commissioned by the children's cultural centre. As a young drama student in 1995, I remember vividly the excitement surrounding the opening of Europe's first ever dedicated children cultural centre. That this ground-breaking innovation was happening in the heart of Dublin city was a source of pride. The Ark Children’s Cultural Centre opened its doors in Temple Bar, three years after the Irish government ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of The Child which recognised the right of children to 'participate freely in cultural life and the arts.’ History was being made. Ireland was showing a new cultural confidence in its vision for investment in both the arts and children. Now, thirty years after its founding, over a million children and their parents and teachers have attended The Ark. Our purpose is to realise children’s right to art and culture with ambition and joy. We do so by commissioning, producing and presenting new art for, by, with and about children from birth to age 12. From the beginning I was inspired by The Ark’s radical approach to art making and community engagement. When I was appointed Director in 2015, I was keen to build on those strong foundations. One of my first projects was to introduce a child participation practice to redistribute decision making power across the organisation alongside a new commissioning strategy. The Ark Children’s Council was established and now plays a key role in all decision-making and inform the development of every new commission. The five writers featured in Dream Big have created new worlds of the imagination.

stories.title: Pat Ingoldsby to sparkle again on spoken-word album
stories.summary: One Good Sparkle, a spoken word album celebrating the life and poetry of the late Pat Ingoldsby, will be digitally released this Monday, with a CD version to follow. Imelda May is among those who will appear on the album, which came about after a funding campaign earlier this year by Athlone-based publishing house Luain Press. He hosted children's TV shows, wrote plays for the stage and radio, published books of short stories and poems and was a newspaper columnist. One Good Sparkle features 18 of Mr Ingoldsby's poems, with Words to the Virus Which Found Me in 1942, (read by the poet himself), the title track (read by Anna D.), and Da Down the Garden (read by Daragh Fleming) already released. The other poems on the album are read by spoken artists Mikey Cullen, Emmet O'Brien, Stephen Maguire, Leon Dunne, Jan Brierton, Stephen James Smith, Ryan Duggins, Lee Sheridan, Annie Peter, David Hynes, Steve O'Toole and Holly Hughes. The readings will be accompanied by music by Welsh pianist and composer Philip May.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (October 9-11)
stories.summary: From a swap shop in Tallaght to a harvest fair in Naul, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. Ready to change up your wardrobe for winter? Swap Til Ye Drop is hosting a sustainably-minded day of shopping at Red Rua in Tallaght on Friday, 9 October, from 5pm-9pm. Bring along up to 10 items of clothes, shoes, accessories and/or books to swap (clean and in good condition). Then you're free to go swapping from what everyone else has brought. Additionally, there will be a repair/upcycling cafe available, so bring along an item or two that needs some TLC. The cast of Pretty Good Improv (Luke Benson, Stephen Bradley, Avril Burke, Niall Johnson, Ross McCarney, Kate Moylan, John Spillane) are teaming up with the cast of Failed State (John Purcell, Malin von Euler-Hogan, and special guest Kelley Quinn of UBC NY) to deliver an unforgettable night of comedy. The show will take place at The Pearse Centre on Friday, 9 October, at 8pm. Tickets €7. Alternative Dublin is hosting a series of spooky social events this October as part of the Dublin Halloween Festival. Their beginner-friendly night of crochet will take place at This Must Be The Place on Saturday, 10 October, at 3pm. You’ll learn how to get comfortable with a crochet hook and yarn, practise basic crochet techniques, and create a handmade pumpkin. All materials are provided. Tickets are €25.64. PIERCED on Camden Street is launching their new Claddagh collection with drinks, snacks, bedazzling, photo ops, discounts & prizes. Taking place on Friday, 9 October, from 5pm-9pm, there will even be a bedazzling station where you can decorate your own Claddagh keyring to take home. €15 ticket, fully redeemable in store on the night. Now in its 21st year, Maths Week runs from Saturday 10th to Saturday 18th October, with events taking place in schools, universities, libraries, visitor centres, parks and even on city streets. Family-friendly events include free outdoor maths trails where children and adults can find and solve puzzles in local parks, as well as exhibits, activities, and more. See the full programme here.

stories.title: Is next Wednesday's public sector strike now inevitable?
stories.summary: The money is there and both sides say they want to do a deal so how are we facing into a massively disruptive public sector strike on Wednesday? More than 300,000 workers including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants will engage in a 24-hour work stoppage and take to the picket lines. It will lead to the closure of schools, the cancellation of hospital appointments and massive disruption to public services. Unions are threatening another strike a week later on 21 October. So how did it come to this? In the early hours of the morning of 26 January 2024, following overnight talks, bleary-eyed trade union negotiators and Government officials emerged from the Workplace Relations Commission to announce that a new public sector pay deal had been agreed. It provided for pay increases of 10.25% and over a two-and-a-half-year period.

stories.title: Job openings down 4.8% in third quarter - Morgan McKinley
stories.summary: Job openings across Ireland were down on an annual basis by 4.8% in the third quarter of the year, according to the latest employment monitor from recruitment firm Morgan McKinley. The research also showed that vacancies are up slightly, by 0.2%, on the previous quarter. Jobseeker registrations rose sharply, up 14% quarter on quarter, and 51% year-on-year. However, according to the report, the increase in jobseeker registrations does not correspond with a rise in unemployment meaning that many workers are exploring opportunities while staying in their current roles. The research found that artificial intelligence is reshaping recruitment, with employers expecting practical AI capability across finance, human resources, marketing and operations. Businesses are also managing a rise in AI-assisted applications, AI-generated CVs and concerns around candidate authenticity.

stories.title: Opposition TDs consider Dáil boycott over strike pickets
stories.summary: Doubt hangs over Wednesday's sitting of the Dáil amid a national day of strike action by public sector workers. Opposition TDs are considering boycotting the sitting should they be required to pass the picket of striking Oireachtas workers. More than 100,000 public sector workers are to take action next week despite a plea in Tuesday's budget speech by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers to engage in dialogue about a new pay deal. In a note to TDs and senators last week, Clerk of the Dáil and Secretary General of the Houses of the Oireachtas Services Elaine Gunn said that Dáil and Seanad sittings, as well as committee hearings, could be affected by any action. It is understood the Houses of the Oireachtas is seeking a derogation to allow its staff to work on Wednesday and to facilitate sittings in both chambers, with a decision on whether it will be granted due tomorrow evening. However, a meeting of the Dáil's Committee on Business heard reservations from opposition TDs about proceeding with Oireachtas business should a derogation not be granted.

stories.title: Delta Air slashes profit forecast over fuel-cost surge
stories.summary: Delta Air Lines cut its annual profit forecast by nearly a quarter today as soaring fuel costs, expected to add $6 billion to its bill in 2026, overwhelmed resilient travel demand and higher ticket prices. Its shares fell 2.5% in early trading after the carrier cut its 2026 profit forecast for the first time this year and lifted its projected fuel-cost increase by $2 billion as the Iran war has driven jet fuel prices sharply higher worldwide. With no end to the war in sight, carriers are confronting their worst crisis since the pandemic. The downgrade underscores a growing challenge for the industry: whether passengers will absorb further fare increases if fuel prices remain elevated. Airlines have already raised fares substantially this year and analysts warn further increases could test travelers' willingness to keep spending. Delta, the first major global carrier to report third-quarter results, said fuel expenses for the period rose 62% from a year earlier to $4.1 billion, exceeding its July forecast by more than $500 million. "All of it's fuel," Delta Chief Financial Officer Erik Snell told reporters when asked what drove the forecast cut, citing increases in both crude oil and refined jet fuel prices since the summer. Delta now expects adjusted annual earnings of $5.10 to $5.60 a share, down from the $6.50 to $7.50 per share it forecast in July. The new midpoint of $5.35 per share is below analysts' average estimate of $5.46 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG. It forecast $4.5 billion in adjusted pre-tax profit for 2026.

stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards have said they have struck a tanker attempting to take an "illegal route" through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has sought to blockade since the outset of the Middle East war. Iranian forces "have taken control of the administration of the strait", the Guards said in a statement carried by the state news agency IRNA. "In carrying out this mission, a few hours ago, a giant LPG carrier named NV Sunshine, owned by NatWit, which was attempting to transit via the illegal route south of the Strait of Hormuz, was struck," it added. Earlier today, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said peace negotiations would only succeed without "pressure and threats". It comes amid deadlocked efforts to end months of fighting in the Middle East. Diplomatic efforts to end the seven-month conflict, which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have been at an impasse since the summer.

stories.title: Meyler: 'Surprised' to see Horan as integration chair
stories.summary: Former Tyrone footballer Conor Meyler has admitted that he was surprised to see former GAA president John Horan named as the new chair of the Steering Group on Integration. The Dubliner was appointed earlier in the week, following the resignation of Dr Mary McAleese from the position. "I'm probably surprised that they went with someone who has a background in the GAA. I know I've been quite vocal before about my own personal opinion and what research steered me, and my supervisory team, towards within the PhD. "That was having an independent chair was the best move, going with something more competency-based, somebody who's come through a process that's been similar in terms of sporting governance, gender reform and merger process. "So I was surprised, (but) I don't know John personally and I have no doubt that he will do a great job. He has obviously come in as well. "This isn't just a GAA decision. The LGFA and Camogie (Association) are obviously all agreed on the decision, which is interesting as well.
